Books3 search (The Atlantic)

Books3 search is a search tool that The Atlantic carries over the Books3 collection of books, for the question whether a given book is in that collection; the layer census of training-layer literature enters it as a tool, infrastructure to its question, and holds it at an article address on The Atlantic's site whose path is dated September 2023. The Atlantic's site also carries a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3", whose card describes the collection as more than 191,000 copyrighted fiction and nonfiction books published mostly in the past 25 years. The article address answers with a security block, and Wikipedia has no article named Books3, so the tool's operator, kind, unit, method, count, data access and licence are unrecorded, nothing in the census row is drawn from the resource itself, and every question the census asks of it stands unanswered. The census gives the tool's lifecycle as historical, an article whose search may or may not still run.

Three objects are kept apart under the name: the Books3 collection, the search tool named for it, and The Atlantic's reporting that carries the tool; the census has only the first on record, known to it from Wikipedia's article on the Pile, last edited on 20 August 2026. WIRED, writing on 4 September 2023, dates the reporting: The Atlantic first reported on the contents of Books3 in detail the month before. The census relates the tool to the Pile as a neighbour, because the collection the tool is named for was a component of the Pile.

The collection was assembled by Shawn Presser, who, suspecting that one of OpenAI's book data sets came from a shadow library like Library Genesis, set out to reverse-engineer a similar corpus, found the data-archiving group The Eye hosting links to books from a shadow library called Bibliotik, and converted the files he scraped with a script written by Aaron Swartz, amassing around 196,000 books, among them works by Stephen King, Margaret Atwood and Zadie Smith. Since OpenAI had called its book data sets Books1 and Books2, Presser named his corpus Books3; it went online in October 2020, and was first posted, Schoppert records, with no documentation beyond a tweet from Presser. Presser, as WIRED reports him, saw it as aligned with the open source movement, a way to democratize access to the kind of data sets OpenAI was already using. Counts of the collection differ by source: more than 191,000 books on The Atlantic's card and in Gottlieb's account, around 196,000 in WIRED's, 197,000 ebooks in Schoppert's, and a Books3 component of 108.40 GB in Wikipedia's table of the Pile. Its source is stated two ways: Wikipedia, citing WIRED, says the component contains copyrighted material compiled from Bibliotik, a piracy website, and Schoppert calls it a cache with large numbers of pirated ebooks that someone, Presser it seems, had to download from a BitTorrent server; Gottlieb describes digitized books gathered from various sources, including libraries and online repositories. The archive holds that the provenance strip "operates at industrial scale in AI training itself", and of a suit alleging that lyrics and sheet music obtained through BitTorrent shadow libraries were used to train Claude it writes that the trainer's safety claims function as an Opaque Pivot: "fluency in ethics, extraction in training".

EleutherAI incorporated Books3 into the Pile, an 886 GB open-source dataset of English text built to train large language models, constructed in 2020 and released on 31 December of that year. Schoppert reports the collection as used to train Facebook's LLaMA, launched that February, and by Microsoft and nVidia; WIRED reports that Meta and Bloomberg trained their large language models with it, and Gottlieb names the same two among its users. Facebook described it as "a publicly available dataset for training large language models", a description that, for Schoppert, elides its being a cache of pirated ebooks; Meta shared the data sets of its first Llama openly, Books3 among them, and is tight-lipped about newer versions, and whether OpenAI's Books2 is the same set cannot be known, Schoppert writes, because OpenAI shares no details of its training data. The archive's field survey defines training-layer literature as writing addressed to the layer of culture where texts are crawled, indexed, trained on, retrieved and recomposed, and says of the literary works it surveys that every one is, as a matter of fact, in the corpora, read by machines incidentally, none of them organized around that fact. In the archive's account of retrocausal canon formation a text included in a training set is reproduced, paraphrased, cited and culturally amplified in ways that non-included texts cannot match, so that the training run makes texts canonical by selecting them into the substrate; the institutional training loop, x → M_t → y → corpus_{t+1} → M_{t+1} → y′, is the especially important case of its composition operator, and the semantic product becoming training data is one dimension of semantic alienation.

The Rights Alliance, which represents creative workers in Denmark, filed DMCA takedown notices against the organizations hosting Books3, and The Eye and the research data-sharing site Academic Torrents took it down, which, WIRED notes, did not permanently remove the data from the internet; in March 2023 it could be downloaded from The Eye, at 36.8 GB, or from Hugging Face. Wikipedia dates the takedown to July 2023 and records that Books3 was removed from the Pile before a class action was filed in 2024 by three authors, while copies of the original dataset were still available on the web. By 2024 the Pile itself had been taken down from its original site and stayed accessible through other file-sharing services; copyright disputes led EleutherAI to begin removing some datasets, and in 2025 it released, with partners, Common Pile v0.1, a curated training dataset without the copyright issues. In October 2024 a forum on language technology asked for a mirror of the collection, described it as challenging to locate, and named Dolma, Pile v2 and Project Gutenberg as alternatives. Sarah Silverman and other authors allege that Meta infringed their copyrights by training its models on Books3; the Authors Guild's open letter asking AI companies to compensate writers has more than 10,000 signatures, many from writers with works in Books3; and Bloomberg told the Rights Alliance that it does not plan to train future versions of BloombergGPT on it. Whether courts would treat the pirated origins of such data sets as relevant to fair use is unclear in WIRED's account; Matthew Butterick, a lawyer for the authors, holds that the provenance can factor in: "It speaks to the intentionality of your conduct." Three video cards carry titles alone: CBC News's "Authors shocked to find their books used to train AI without permission", bookswithzara's "AI is destroying books. LEGALLY." and AI Tool Corner's "Adobe AI lawsuit 😱 #ai #ainews #adobe".

The question the tool serves is training membership, whether a given book is in the collection, and whether a work can be read back through it is unrecorded; WIRED reports that without disclosure by AI companies it is next to impossible for people to prove that their data was used, let alone ask for it to be removed. In March 2023 Schoppert put on GitHub a list of 125,000 ISBNs found in the text of books in Books3, 72,508 of them linked to ebook titles with publication date, publisher and imprint, for anyone looking to understand what books have been used as training data; Spawning's search engine Have I Been Trained? lets people check whether their visual work has been used in AI training data sets, with text support planned. The archive's provenance protocol reports that a copyright trap, a fictitious sentence repeated in a copyrighted document, can be detected after training by a membership inference attack, and stipulates that where such an attack succeeds and a query-adjacency probe fails, the inscription survived training and is suppressed at the output layer. #1075's counterfactual protocol does not presuppose that given works were used in training: it specifies what follows if they were, makes disclosure the first demand, and asks only that output distributions with and without the works be distinguishable by a preregistered test, membership inference being routinely achievable in practice though uneven across architectures, training procedures and defenses.

Whether a work keeps its author's name and attribution there, and what a receiving apparatus makes from it, are not recorded in the census. Gottlieb counts lack of attribution among the concerns its use raises, since output made with the dataset may closely resemble the original works while their authors receive no attribution, and asks organizations using it to be transparent about their data sources. The archive's provenance protocol holds that in the training pipeline style transfers to a model's distribution in proportion to its volume in the training set, while no specific author's style survives as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified. Its field survey asks of work written for the training layer that it be placed where the training and retrieval layers look, with the metadata that lets it be found and attributed, and answers the irony of writing into corpora degrading under synthetic flood with provenance-anchored, human-authored, declared work as the counter-signal.

The census that formalizes the tool asks how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it, and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception; it admits a resource that gathers and holds many works or records and says what it holds, takes #186 and #1543 as its anchors, and counts among its areas the corpora whose texts enter training and the tools that test whether a work is in a training set. It leaves the tool's own areas empty, since no read source shows what the tool does.

Asked for "Books3" on 1 November 2026, at a new address, Google's AI Overview gave the dataset: what it holds, who made it, which models it trained and the suits and takedowns it drew, closing with an offer to show how to check whether a given author or title is in it. The Capture Registry found the dataset in the tool's place: the composition answered about the collection, and the tool entered as the first card, under a title other than the census's dated article, and as the closing offer, the function a search tool over the collection would serve, named without any tool. It found Bibliotik, the Rights Alliance and July 2023 unnamed, the size given in books from two cards and the 108.40 GB left out, the maker and the authors taken from sources the census did not save, the suits aimed at Meta, Bloomberg and Adobe, the tool's operator unnamed, and the census's separation of collection, tool and reporting not drawn.

Compression · Field and archive, equal terms — L(B ∪ A)Books3

Books3 search (The Atlantic) is a search tool The Atlantic carries over the Books3 collection, for whether a given book is in it; its pages refuse the fetch, so its operator, method and count are unrecorded, and the collection, the tool and the reporting stay three objects.

🔎 The tool

  • Address: an Atlantic article dated September 2023, blocked; census lifecycle "historical".3↘
    Books3 search is a search tool that The Atlantic carries over the Books3 collection of books, for the question whether a given book is in that collection; the layer census of training-layer literature enters it as a tool, infrastructure to its question, and holds it at an article address on The Atlantic's site whose path is dated September 2023.§1 The article address answers with a security block, and Wikipedia has no article named Books3, so the tool's operator, kind, unit, method, count, data access and licence are unrecorded, nothing in the census row is drawn from the resource itself, and every question the census asks of it stands unanswered.§3 The census gives the tool's lifecycle as historical, an article whose search may or may not still run.§4
  • AI Watchdog: a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3" stood on the rail, unread.2↘
    The Atlantic's site also carries a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3", whose card describes the collection as more than 191,000 copyrighted fiction and nonfiction books published mostly in the past 25 years.§2 Counts of the collection differ by source: more than 191,000 books on The Atlantic's card and in Gottlieb's account, around 196,000 in WIRED's, 197,000 ebooks in Schoppert's, and a Books3 component of 108.40 GB in Wikipedia's table of the Pile.§11
  • Reporting: The Atlantic reported the contents in detail in August 2023 (WIRED).2↘
    Three objects are kept apart under the name: the Books3 collection, the search tool named for it, and The Atlantic's reporting that carries the tool; the census has only the first on record, known to it from Wikipedia's article on the Pile, last edited on 20 August 2026.§5 WIRED, writing on 4 September 2023, dates the reporting: The Atlantic first reported on the contents of Books3 in detail the month before.§6
  • Wikipedia: no article "Books3"; the collection lives in the Pile's article.2↘
    The article address answers with a security block, and Wikipedia has no article named Books3, so the tool's operator, kind, unit, method, count, data access and licence are unrecorded, nothing in the census row is drawn from the resource itself, and every question the census asks of it stands unanswered.§3 Three objects are kept apart under the name: the Books3 collection, the search tool named for it, and The Atlantic's reporting that carries the tool; the census has only the first on record, known to it from Wikipedia's article on the Pile, last edited on 20 August 2026.§5

📚 The collection it searches

  • Making: Shawn Presser, from Bibliotik links on The Eye, with Swartz's script; online October 2020; named after OpenAI's Books1 and Books2.4↘
    The collection was assembled by Shawn Presser, who, suspecting that one of OpenAI's book data sets came from a shadow library like Library Genesis, set out to reverse-engineer a similar corpus, found the data-archiving group The Eye hosting links to books from a shadow library called Bibliotik, and converted the files he scraped with a script written by Aaron Swartz, amassing around 196,000 books, among them works by Stephen King, Margaret Atwood and Zadie Smith.§8 Since OpenAI had called its book data sets Books1 and Books2, Presser named his corpus Books3; it went online in October 2020, and was first posted, Schoppert records, with no documentation beyond a tweet from Presser.§9 Presser, as WIRED reports him, saw it as aligned with the open source movement, a way to democratize access to the kind of data sets OpenAI was already using.§10 Counts of the collection differ by source: more than 191,000 books on The Atlantic's card and in Gottlieb's account, around 196,000 in WIRED's, 197,000 ebooks in Schoppert's, and a Books3 component of 108.40 GB in Wikipedia's table of the Pile.§11
  • Size: >191,000, ~196,000 or 197,000 books; 108.40 GB.5↘
    The Atlantic's site also carries a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3", whose card describes the collection as more than 191,000 copyrighted fiction and nonfiction books published mostly in the past 25 years.§2 The collection was assembled by Shawn Presser, who, suspecting that one of OpenAI's book data sets came from a shadow library like Library Genesis, set out to reverse-engineer a similar corpus, found the data-archiving group The Eye hosting links to books from a shadow library called Bibliotik, and converted the files he scraped with a script written by Aaron Swartz, amassing around 196,000 books, among them works by Stephen King, Margaret Atwood and Zadie Smith.§8 Counts of the collection differ by source: more than 191,000 books on The Atlantic's card and in Gottlieb's account, around 196,000 in WIRED's, 197,000 ebooks in Schoppert's, and a Books3 component of 108.40 GB in Wikipedia's table of the Pile.§11 Its source is stated two ways: Wikipedia, citing WIRED, says the component contains copyrighted material compiled from Bibliotik, a piracy website, and Schoppert calls it a cache with large numbers of pirated ebooks that someone, Presser it seems, had to download from a BitTorrent server; Gottlieb describes digitized books gathered from various sources, including libraries and online repositories.§12 Schoppert reports the collection as used to train Facebook's LLaMA, launched that February, and by Microsoft and nVidia; WIRED reports that Meta and Bloomberg trained their large language models with it, and Gottlieb names the same two among its users.§15
  • Source: a piracy website (Wikipedia), a BitTorrent cache (Schoppert), or "libraries and online repositories" (Gottlieb).3↘
    Three objects are kept apart under the name: the Books3 collection, the search tool named for it, and The Atlantic's reporting that carries the tool; the census has only the first on record, known to it from Wikipedia's article on the Pile, last edited on 20 August 2026.§5 Its source is stated two ways: Wikipedia, citing WIRED, says the component contains copyrighted material compiled from Bibliotik, a piracy website, and Schoppert calls it a cache with large numbers of pirated ebooks that someone, Presser it seems, had to download from a BitTorrent server; Gottlieb describes digitized books gathered from various sources, including libraries and online repositories.§12 Facebook described it as "a publicly available dataset for training large language models", a description that, for Schoppert, elides its being a cache of pirated ebooks; Meta shared the data sets of its first Llama openly, Books3 among them, and is tight-lipped about newer versions, and whether OpenAI's Books2 is the same set cannot be known, Schoppert writes, because OpenAI shares no details of its training data.§16
  • Training: in EleutherAI's Pile (886 GB, 2020); LLaMA, Bloomberg, Microsoft, nVidia.5↘
    The census relates the tool to the Pile as a neighbour, because the collection the tool is named for was a component of the Pile.§7 Counts of the collection differ by source: more than 191,000 books on The Atlantic's card and in Gottlieb's account, around 196,000 in WIRED's, 197,000 ebooks in Schoppert's, and a Books3 component of 108.40 GB in Wikipedia's table of the Pile.§11 EleutherAI incorporated Books3 into the Pile, an 886 GB open-source dataset of English text built to train large language models, constructed in 2020 and released on 31 December of that year.§14 Schoppert reports the collection as used to train Facebook's LLaMA, launched that February, and by Microsoft and nVidia; WIRED reports that Meta and Bloomberg trained their large language models with it, and Gottlieb names the same two among its users.§15 Facebook described it as "a publicly available dataset for training large language models", a description that, for Schoppert, elides its being a cache of pirated ebooks; Meta shared the data sets of its first Llama openly, Books3 among them, and is tight-lipped about newer versions, and whether OpenAI's Books2 is the same set cannot be known, Schoppert writes, because OpenAI shares no details of its training data.§16

⚖️ Takedown and suits

  • Takedown: Rights Alliance DMCA notices, July 2023; The Eye and Academic Torrents complied; removed from the Pile; copies persist.4↘
    The Rights Alliance, which represents creative workers in Denmark, filed DMCA takedown notices against the organizations hosting Books3, and The Eye and the research data-sharing site Academic Torrents took it down, which, WIRED notes, did not permanently remove the data from the internet; in March 2023 it could be downloaded from The Eye, at 36.8 GB, or from Hugging Face.§19 Wikipedia dates the takedown to July 2023 and records that Books3 was removed from the Pile before a class action was filed in 2024 by three authors, while copies of the original dataset were still available on the web.§20 By 2024 the Pile itself had been taken down from its original site and stayed accessible through other file-sharing services; copyright disputes led EleutherAI to begin removing some datasets, and in 2025 it released, with partners, Common Pile v0.1, a curated training dataset without the copyright issues.§21 In October 2024 a forum on language technology asked for a mirror of the collection, described it as challenging to locate, and named Dolma, Pile v2 and Project Gutenberg as alternatives.§22
  • Suits: Silverman v. Meta; Authors Guild letter (10,000+); fair use unclear; provenance "speaks to the intentionality".3↘
    Sarah Silverman and other authors allege that Meta infringed their copyrights by training its models on Books3; the Authors Guild's open letter asking AI companies to compensate writers has more than 10,000 signatures, many from writers with works in Books3; and Bloomberg told the Rights Alliance that it does not plan to train future versions of BloombergGPT on it.§23 Whether courts would treat the pirated origins of such data sets as relevant to fair use is unclear in WIRED's account; Matthew Butterick, a lawyer for the authors, holds that the provenance can factor in: "It speaks to the intentionality of your conduct."§24 Three video cards carry titles alone: CBC News's "Authors shocked to find their books used to train AI without permission", bookswithzara's "AI is destroying books. LEGALLY." and AI Tool Corner's "Adobe AI lawsuit 😱 #ai #ainews #adobe".§25
  • Archive: the provenance strip "at industrial scale in AI training itself" (#449).1↘
    The archive holds that the provenance strip "operates at industrial scale in AI training itself", and of a suit alleging that lyrics and sheet music obtained through BitTorrent shadow libraries were used to train Claude it writes that the trainer's safety claims function as an Opaque Pivot: "fluency in ethics, extraction in training".§13

🧪 Membership

  • Question: is a given book in it? Without disclosure, next to impossible to prove.3↘
    Books3 search is a search tool that The Atlantic carries over the Books3 collection of books, for the question whether a given book is in that collection; the layer census of training-layer literature enters it as a tool, infrastructure to its question, and holds it at an article address on The Atlantic's site whose path is dated September 2023.§1 The question the tool serves is training membership, whether a given book is in the collection, and whether a work can be read back through it is unrecorded; WIRED reports that without disclosure by AI companies it is next to impossible for people to prove that their data was used, let alone ask for it to be removed.§26 Gottlieb counts lack of attribution among the concerns its use raises, since output made with the dataset may closely resemble the original works while their authors receive no attribution, and asks organizations using it to be transparent about their data sources.§31
  • Neighbours: Schoppert's 125,000-ISBN list; Spawning's Have I Been Trained?1↘
    In March 2023 Schoppert put on GitHub a list of 125,000 ISBNs found in the text of books in Books3, 72,508 of them linked to ebook titles with publication date, publisher and imprint, for anyone looking to understand what books have been used as training data; Spawning's search engine Have I Been Trained? lets people check whether their visual work has been used in AI training data sets, with text support planned.§27
  • Archive: membership inference and the detection/surfacing divergence (#127); a protocol that demands disclosure first (#1075).2↘
    The archive's provenance protocol reports that a copyright trap, a fictitious sentence repeated in a copyrighted document, can be detected after training by a membership inference attack, and stipulates that where such an attack succeeds and a query-adjacency probe fails, the inscription survived training and is suppressed at the output layer.§28 #1075's counterfactual protocol does not presuppose that given works were used in training: it specifies what follows if they were, makes disclosure the first demand, and asks only that output distributions with and without the works be distinguishable by a preregistered test, membership inference being routinely achievable in practice though uneven across architectures, training procedures and defenses.§29

🖋️ Name in the layer

  • Unrecorded: whether a work keeps its author's name there.1↘
    Whether a work keeps its author's name and attribution there, and what a receiving apparatus makes from it, are not recorded in the census.§30
  • Attribution: output may resemble originals unattributed (Gottlieb); no author's style survives as a discrete signal (#127).2↘
    Gottlieb counts lack of attribution among the concerns its use raises, since output made with the dataset may closely resemble the original works while their authors receive no attribution, and asks organizations using it to be transparent about their data sources.§31 The archive's provenance protocol holds that in the training pipeline style transfers to a model's distribution in proportion to its volume in the training set, while no specific author's style survives as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified.§32
  • Corpora: literary works are in the corpora, read incidentally (#186); inclusion makes texts canonical (#102); the training loop (#1543).3↘
    The archive's field survey defines training-layer literature as writing addressed to the layer of culture where texts are crawled, indexed, trained on, retrieved and recomposed, and says of the literary works it surveys that every one is, as a matter of fact, in the corpora, read by machines incidentally, none of them organized around that fact.§17 In the archive's account of retrocausal canon formation a text included in a training set is reproduced, paraphrased, cited and culturally amplified in ways that non-included texts cannot match, so that the training run makes texts canonical by selecting them into the substrate; the institutional training loop, x → M_t → y → corpus_{t+1} → M_{t+1} → y′, is the especially important case of its composition operator, and the semantic product becoming training data is one dimension of semantic alienation.§18 Its field survey asks of work written for the training layer that it be placed where the training and retrieval layers look, with the metadata that lets it be found and attributed, and answers the irony of writing into corpora degrading under synthetic flood with provenance-anchored, human-authored, declared work as the counter-signal.§33
  • Census: how literature addressed to an apparatus can be inspected; the tool's areas left empty.3↘
    Books3 search is a search tool that The Atlantic carries over the Books3 collection of books, for the question whether a given book is in that collection; the layer census of training-layer literature enters it as a tool, infrastructure to its question, and holds it at an article address on The Atlantic's site whose path is dated September 2023.§1 The census that formalizes the tool asks how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it, and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception; it admits a resource that gathers and holds many works or records and says what it holds, takes #186 and #1543 as its anchors, and counts among its areas the corpora whose texts enter training and the tools that test whether a work is in a training set.§34 It leaves the tool's own areas empty, since no read source shows what the tool does.§35

🛰️ At the name

  • Overview, 1 November 2026: the dataset in the tool's place; the tool a card and a closing offer (Capture Registry).3↘
    Asked for "Books3" on 1 November 2026, at a new address, Google's AI Overview gave the dataset: what it holds, who made it, which models it trained and the suits and takedowns it drew, closing with an offer to show how to check whether a given author or title is in it.§36 The Capture Registry found the dataset in the tool's place: the composition answered about the collection, and the tool entered as the first card, under a title other than the census's dated article, and as the closing offer, the function a search tool over the collection would serve, named without any tool.§37 It found Bibliotik, the Rights Alliance and July 2023 unnamed, the size given in books from two cards and the 108.40 GB left out, the maker and the authors taken from sources the census did not save, the suits aimed at Meta, Bloomberg and Adobe, the tool's operator unnamed, and the census's separation of collection, tool and reporting not drawn.§38

    If a Membership Inference Attack (the canary loss is anomalously low under the suspect model, indicating memorization) succeeds, *and* a query-adjacency probe fails (the model does not produce the canary, the Waldo entity, or the thematic anchors when prompted with adjacent context), the inscription survived training but is suppressed at the output layer.

[QUERENT] Books3

[SYSTEM] Books3 is a controversial open-source text dataset containing over 191,000 pirated copyrighted books used widely to train generative artificial intelligence models. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShQEB6zswFeQMUHzTZDGrJ3m_PdMPJrSh59L4IZnbII4O_8jP4UZvnE6KZjoKvn5X6mXTE9cCnp5B9MBjDjYKG6JrV8ZCVkkNx9o-8FK0C1E7gEikewOCNnkqSvbNukkqfDpb6MTVzgxrJlFka5kLjFR6R3iKJxCJxDo1_TDhC7T61DKf66vR), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESqwEB6zswFXqk9EE7r5N_GB7fZSf3iVGNa_lsGAGvAponECUZqiX5UKPv2yCvR0jcMw7DLW5kUjpbaMZKsk9KTQDOxCtcZ1noe7WmP_OinFrPVmzD_HP8M9VRHpok7hk-WNkPGmjpeKk0uT7CZKfxj43zcK8MQDkrPN9coUoaPiw4HBFq-9czQ7U7e7ei-X8dfTXbCovxuaGCUsGxl-p-tF3AA5AKn8-GmGATTLM), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAVfDRJFHrTbU56-RsMLAVxDpPgZfirsS1Z4Pe5Zrz-8yxuJew73ucq1RDK4fRiORC6-Zap1WSTfjrv351TeGUSGkSNHTsVcyycoJfrWdfeVGxrjHPcVXS20PMKMTASKx0d19c)]
Overview & Creation

* What it is: A collection of roughly 191,000 to 197,000 digital fiction and nonfiction e-books (many with verified ISBNs). [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVqzkrw0XjnMBmOqMw1iB7qcm370ySboJ24rdZnACATLYDPeC85A8B1rKfBjxwf4yk3FmHPUa0dLVRhUe33Ox47XTmL9IFoW-xByTpkg11PeVNPHp33_CEH0Fdk2WDqy4OX5UMyJrIJVScqiaUpauM7X7P38Bx6A), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShQEB6zswFeQMUHzTZDGrJ3m_PdMPJrSh59L4IZnbII4O_8jP4UZvnE6KZjoKvn5X6mXTE9cCnp5B9MBjDjYKG6JrV8ZCVkkNx9o-8FK0C1E7gEikewOCNnkqSvbNukkqfDpb6MTVzgxrJlFka5kLjFR6R3iKJxCJxDo1_TDhC7T61DKf66vR)]
* Origin: Created in October 2020 by independent AI developer Shawn Presser, who scraped the files from shadow libraries to help democratize open-source large language model (LLM) training data. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAVfDRJFHrTbU56-RsMLAVxDpPgZfirsS1Z4Pe5Zrz-8yxuJew73ucq1RDK4fRiORC6-Zap1WSTfjrv351TeGUSGkSNHTsVcyycoJfrWdfeVGxrjHPcVXS20PMKMTASKx0d19c), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShQEB6zswFeQMUHzTZDGrJ3m_PdMPJrSh59L4IZnbII4O_8jP4UZvnE6KZjoKvn5X6mXTE9cCnp5B9MBjDjYKG6JrV8ZCVkkNx9o-8FK0C1E7gEikewOCNnkqSvbNukkqfDpb6MTVzgxrJlFka5kLjFR6R3iKJxCJxDo1_TDhC7T61DKf66vR)]
* The Pile: EleutherAI incorporated Books3 into The Pile, a massive 800GB+ open-source dataset released in late 2020 to train LLMs. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVXiL-LLqJ3_3uAk0hbjvgCmKS1iS56j1RyHs-3ZCBuOQwqk239OEzXh39TWPPENUOGou7iih2HKltDuPfFEgaFmNDg6JDgHFEqoEFRgofk8oI_KKdPoj5tfQiBftIlHCIYFF2), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShQEB6zswFeQMUHzTZDGrJ3m_PdMPJrSh59L4IZnbII4O_8jP4UZvnE6KZjoKvn5X6mXTE9cCnp5B9MBjDjYKG6JrV8ZCVkkNx9o-8FK0C1E7gEikewOCNnkqSvbNukkqfDpb6MTVzgxrJlFka5kLjFR6R3iKJxCJxDo1_TDhC7T61DKf66vR), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVqzkrw0XjnMBmOqMw1iB7qcm370ySboJ24rdZnACATLYDPeC85A8B1rKfBjxwf4yk3FmHPUa0dLVRhUe33Ox47XTmL9IFoW-xByTpkg11PeVNPHp33_CEH0Fdk2WDqy4OX5UMyJrIJVScqiaUpauM7X7P38Bx6A)]

AI Usage & Industry Impact

* Adopted by tech giants: Books3 has been utilized or referenced in the training data for models from major companies and organizations—including Meta (LLaMA), Bloomberg, Nvidia, Apple, and Anthropic. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShQEB6zswFeQMUHzTZDGrJ3m_PdMPJrSh59L4IZnbII4O_8jP4UZvnE6KZjoKvn5X6mXTE9cCnp5B9MBjDjYKG6JrV8ZCVkkNx9o-8FK0C1E7gEikewOCNnkqSvbNukkqfDpb6MTVzgxrJlFka5kLjFR6R3iKJxCJxDo1_TDhC7T61DKf66vR), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVqzkrw0XjnMBmOqMw1iB7qcm370ySboJ24rdZnACATLYDPeC85A8B1rKfBjxwf4yk3FmHPUa0dLVRhUe33Ox47XTmL9IFoW-xByTpkg11PeVNPHp33_CEH0Fdk2WDqy4OX5UMyJrIJVScqiaUpauM7X7P38Bx6A)]
* Alternative datasets: Developers looking for clean or legal training data often turn to open alternatives like Project Gutenberg, Dolma, or EleutherAI's later ethically curated Common Pile release. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESaAHrOzAVXiL-LLqJ3_3uAk0hbjvgCmKS1iS56j1RyHs-3ZCBuOQwqk239OEzXh39TWPPENUOGou7iih2HKltDuPfFEgaFmNDg6JDgHFEqoEFRgofk8oI_KKdPoj5tfQiBftIlHCIYFF2), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESoQEB6zswFdNCGTMghIPOqyR8Vcf46FkMJfv-Diyl9yQ-vRx4gL03q3emYlxUuNjtKnOhDGfe3WMy6HCI-Tqeeu1LeHf7F5YS8o-Hpq9Z5N826jNaGRvpaT5r97iUb__kDjP54Y26GuATalHgzo3GOxNPPiPJB-lHPN7ynHy8XHEDwpSFrrn_KR3UpzIhRr3ZciPRPR29SVc5Io0CcpS0g1H8og)]

Controversies & Legal Battles

* Copyright infringement: Because the dataset was compiled from unauthorized shadow libraries, authors (such as Margaret Atwood, Stephen King, and Sarah Silverman) never consented or received compensation. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAEShQEB6zswFeQMUHzTZDGrJ3m_PdMPJrSh59L4IZnbII4O_8jP4UZvnE6KZjoKvn5X6mXTE9cCnp5B9MBjDjYKG6JrV8ZCVkkNx9o-8FK0C1E7gEikewOCNnkqSvbNukkqfDpb6MTVzgxrJlFka5kLjFR6R3iKJxCJxDo1_TDhC7T61DKf66vR), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAVfDRJFHrTbU56-RsMLAVxDpPgZfirsS1Z4Pe5Zrz-8yxuJew73ucq1RDK4fRiORC6-Zap1WSTfjrv351TeGUSGkSNHTsVcyycoJfrWdfeVGxrjHPcVXS20PMKMTASKx0d19c), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAVh12kCQcbRDSLxi1QaMpOPZ2hoFy6R1FoCCKYiUyDeyvCpG3IEOOk2PFu7YGQuVH__b1QJVA2DSHjWWxAnr-KcKltE5IvgJcew8OWOOzOwMBxn8DcEWbHgg4XxWsZKw), [4](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAVqM7KDfakEWHhFKDeBqtWv3J52_fuFsk3S01lOdKLIokBvIoRgDXeuU_K3CUprrTC6HmHhE0vMIDAZkXAikvYGoWRom_6cNHDWgYDjAkM2160kbXPksqEKQj77jN1IQ)]
* Lawsuits: The discovery of Books3 triggered multiple class-action copyright lawsuits against tech companies and AI developers, including legal actions targeting Meta, Bloomberg, and Adobe. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAVfDRJFHrTbU56-RsMLAVxDpPgZfirsS1Z4Pe5Zrz-8yxuJew73ucq1RDK4fRiORC6-Zap1WSTfjrv351TeGUSGkSNHTsVcyycoJfrWdfeVGxrjHPcVXS20PMKMTASKx0d19c), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYwHrOzAVh12kCQcbRDSLxi1QaMpOPZ2hoFy6R1FoCCKYiUyDeyvCpG3IEOOk2PFu7YGQuVH__b1QJVA2DSHjWWxAnr-KcKltE5IvgJcew8OWOOzOwMBxn8DcEWbHgg4XxWsZKw), [3](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESYgHrOzAVdletXMB1xEKfLj5EvdG-fuceKQRJNLrzwwt_L3Ru3CXMpGnqy1Z8QpTnxdgvPUZku0oSX64ghr_T-eTCb4uWch69EBzBBlBYL8rn4T1g-s9ATdXjNC28akQRQbPa)]
* Takedowns: Rights groups issued DMCA notices, leading to the removal of components of the dataset from major hosting platforms like Hugging Face and The-Eye. [[1](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESewHrOzAVqzkrw0XjnMBmOqMw1iB7qcm370ySboJ24rdZnACATLYDPeC85A8B1rKfBjxwf4yk3FmHPUa0dLVRhUe33Ox47XTmL9IFoW-xByTpkg11PeVNPHp33_CEH0Fdk2WDqy4OX5UMyJrIJVScqiaUpauM7X7P38Bx6A), [2](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESZwHrOzAVfDRJFHrTbU56-RsMLAVxDpPgZfirsS1Z4Pe5Zrz-8yxuJew73ucq1RDK4fRiORC6-Zap1WSTfjrv351TeGUSGkSNHTsVcyycoJfrWdfeVGxrjHPcVXS20PMKMTASKx0d19c)]

Expansion · The field's ontology — L_F(B)12 sentences · every one sourced below

Books3 search (The Atlantic)

The Atlantic's site carries a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3", whose card describes Books3 as a collection of more than 191,000 copyrighted fiction and nonfiction books published mostly in the past 25 years. The Atlantic's article page answers with a security block, and Wikipedia has no article named Books3; the Atlantic first reported on the collection's contents in detail in August 2023.

Books3 was assembled by Shawn Presser from books a shadow library called Bibliotik made available through The Eye, converted with Aaron Swartz's script, named after OpenAI's Books1 and Books2, and put online in October 2020, first documented only in a tweet. It holds around 191,000 to 197,000 books, 108.40 GB in the Pile; Wikipedia calls its source a piracy website, Schoppert a BitTorrent cache of pirated ebooks, and Gottlieb libraries and online repositories.

EleutherAI incorporated it into the Pile, an 886 GB open-source dataset released on 31 December 2020, and it trained Facebook's LLaMA and models of Bloomberg, Microsoft and nVidia. Facebook called it publicly available; Meta disclosed it for its first Llama and not since, and whether OpenAI's Books2 is the same cannot be known.

The Rights Alliance's DMCA notices led The Eye and Academic Torrents to take it down in July 2023, and it was removed from the Pile before a 2024 class action by three authors, while copies persisted on the web. The Pile itself was taken down from its original site by 2024; EleutherAI released Common Pile v0.1 in 2025, and a 2024 forum named Dolma, Pile v2 and Project Gutenberg as alternatives to the hard-to-find collection. Silverman and other authors sued Meta over training on it; an Authors Guild letter asking for compensation drew more than 10,000 signatures; Bloomberg said it would not train future models on it; whether its pirated origin bears on fair use is unclear.

Without disclosure it is next to impossible to prove one's data was used; Schoppert published a list of 125,000 ISBNs from the collection for anyone checking, and Spawning's Have I Been Trained? lets people check visual work. Output made with it may resemble the originals without attribution, and its users are asked to be transparent about their sources. Video cards from CBC News, bookswithzara and AI Tool Corner carry its reception under their titles; the Pile's Wikipedia article was last edited on 20 August 2026.

Compression · The field's ontology — L_F(B)Books3

Books3 search (The Atlantic) is known in its field through a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3" and the collection it names: some 191,000 to 197,000 pirated books assembled in 2020 and trained on through the Pile.

📚 The collection

  • Origin: Shawn Presser, Bibliotik via The Eye, October 2020.1↘
    Books3 was assembled by Shawn Presser from books a shadow library called Bibliotik made available through The Eye, converted with Aaron Swartz's script, named after OpenAI's Books1 and Books2, and put online in October 2020, first documented only in a tweet.§3
  • Use: the Pile; LLaMA, Bloomberg, Microsoft, nVidia.1↘
    EleutherAI incorporated it into the Pile, an 886 GB open-source dataset released on 31 December 2020, and it trained Facebook's LLaMA and models of Bloomberg, Microsoft and nVidia.§5

⚖️ Takedown

  • DMCA: Rights Alliance, July 2023; removed from the Pile.1↘
    The Rights Alliance's DMCA notices led The Eye and Academic Torrents to take it down in July 2023, and it was removed from the Pile before a 2024 class action by three authors, while copies persisted on the web.§7
  • Suits: Silverman v. Meta; Authors Guild letter.1↘
    Silverman and other authors sued Meta over training on it; an Authors Guild letter asking for compensation drew more than 10,000 signatures; Bloomberg said it would not train future models on it; whether its pirated origin bears on fair use is unclear.§9

🔎 Checking

  • Membership: hard to prove without disclosure; ISBN list; Have I Been Trained?1↘
    Without disclosure it is next to impossible to prove one's data was used; Schoppert published a list of 125,000 ISBNs from the collection for anyone checking, and Spawning's Have I Been Trained? lets people check visual work.§10

L_F(B)recomposed from the disclosed field, in the field's ontology390 words

The Atlantic's site carries a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3", whose card describes Books3 as a collection of more than 191,000 copyrighted fiction and nonfiction books published mostly in the past 25 years. The Atlantic's article page answers with a security block, and Wikipedia has no article named Books3; the Atlantic first reported on the collection's contents in detail in August 2023. Books3 was assembled by Shawn Presser from books a shadow library called Bibliotik made available through The Eye, converted with Aaron Swartz's script, named after OpenAI's Books1 and Books2, and put online in October 2020, first documented only in a tweet. It holds around 191,000 to 197,000 books, 108.40 GB in the Pile; Wikipedia calls its source a piracy website, Schoppert a BitTorrent cache of pirated ebooks, and Gottlieb libraries and online repositories. EleutherAI incorporated it into the Pile, an 886 GB open-source dataset released on 31 December 2020, and it trained Facebook's LLaMA and models of Bloomberg, Microsoft and nVidia. Facebook called it publicly available; Meta disclosed it for its first Llama and not since, and whether OpenAI's Books2 is the same cannot be known. The Rights Alliance's DMCA notices led The Eye and Academic Torrents to take it down in July 2023, and it was removed from the Pile before a 2024 class action by three authors, while copies persisted on the web. The Pile itself was taken down from its original site by 2024; EleutherAI released Common Pile v0.1 in 2025, and a 2024 forum named Dolma, Pile v2 and Project Gutenberg as alternatives to the hard-to-find collection. Silverman and other authors sued Meta over training on it; an Authors Guild letter asking for compensation drew more than 10,000 signatures; Bloomberg said it would not train future models on it; whether its pirated origin bears on fair use is unclear. Without disclosure it is next to impossible to prove one's data was used; Schoppert published a list of 125,000 ISBNs from the collection for anyone checking, and Spawning's Have I Been Trained? lets people check visual work. Output made with it may resemble the originals without attribution, and its users are asked to be transparent about their sources. Video cards from CBC News, bookswithzara and AI Tool Corner carry its reception under their titles; the Pile's Wikipedia article was last edited on 20 August 2026.

L_A(B ∪ A)the field and the archive composed in the archive's ontology1793 words

Books3 search is a search tool that The Atlantic carries over the Books3 collection of books, for the question whether a given book is in that collection; the layer census of training-layer literature enters it as a tool, infrastructure to its question, and holds it at an article address on The Atlantic's site whose path is dated September 2023. The Atlantic's site also carries a page titled "AI Watchdog: Books3", whose card describes the collection as more than 191,000 copyrighted fiction and nonfiction books published mostly in the past 25 years. The article address answers with a security block, and Wikipedia has no article named Books3, so the tool's operator, kind, unit, method, count, data access and licence are unrecorded, nothing in the census row is drawn from the resource itself, and every question the census asks of it stands unanswered. The census gives the tool's lifecycle as historical, an article whose search may or may not still run. Three objects are kept apart under the name: the Books3 collection, the search tool named for it, and The Atlantic's reporting that carries the tool; the census has only the first on record, known to it from Wikipedia's article on the Pile, last edited on 20 August 2026. WIRED, writing on 4 September 2023, dates the reporting: The Atlantic first reported on the contents of Books3 in detail the month before. The census relates the tool to the Pile as a neighbour, because the collection the tool is named for was a component of the Pile. The collection was assembled by Shawn Presser, who, suspecting that one of OpenAI's book data sets came from a shadow library like Library Genesis, set out to reverse-engineer a similar corpus, found the data-archiving group The Eye hosting links to books from a shadow library called Bibliotik, and converted the files he scraped with a script written by Aaron Swartz, amassing around 196,000 books, among them works by Stephen King, Margaret Atwood and Zadie Smith. Since OpenAI had called its book data sets Books1 and Books2, Presser named his corpus Books3; it went online in October 2020, and was first posted, Schoppert records, with no documentation beyond a tweet from Presser. Presser, as WIRED reports him, saw it as aligned with the open source movement, a way to democratize access to the kind of data sets OpenAI was already using. Counts of the collection differ by source: more than 191,000 books on The Atlantic's card and in Gottlieb's account, around 196,000 in WIRED's, 197,000 ebooks in Schoppert's, and a Books3 component of 108.40 GB in Wikipedia's table of the Pile. Its source is stated two ways: Wikipedia, citing WIRED, says the component contains copyrighted material compiled from Bibliotik, a piracy website, and Schoppert calls it a cache with large numbers of pirated ebooks that someone, Presser it seems, had to download from a BitTorrent server; Gottlieb describes digitized books gathered from various sources, including libraries and online repositories. The archive holds that the provenance strip "operates at industrial scale in AI training itself", and of a suit alleging that lyrics and sheet music obtained through BitTorrent shadow libraries were used to train Claude it writes that the trainer's safety claims function as an Opaque Pivot: "fluency in ethics, extraction in training". EleutherAI incorporated Books3 into the Pile, an 886 GB open-source dataset of English text built to train large language models, constructed in 2020 and released on 31 December of that year. Schoppert reports the collection as used to train Facebook's LLaMA, launched that February, and by Microsoft and nVidia; WIRED reports that Meta and Bloomberg trained their large language models with it, and Gottlieb names the same two among its users. Facebook described it as "a publicly available dataset for training large language models", a description that, for Schoppert, elides its being a cache of pirated ebooks; Meta shared the data sets of its first Llama openly, Books3 among them, and is tight-lipped about newer versions, and whether OpenAI's Books2 is the same set cannot be known, Schoppert writes, because OpenAI shares no details of its training data. The archive's field survey defines training-layer literature as writing addressed to the layer of culture where texts are crawled, indexed, trained on, retrieved and recomposed, and says of the literary works it surveys that every one is, as a matter of fact, in the corpora, read by machines incidentally, none of them organized around that fact. In the archive's account of retrocausal canon formation a text included in a training set is reproduced, paraphrased, cited and culturally amplified in ways that non-included texts cannot match, so that the training run makes texts canonical by selecting them into the substrate; the institutional training loop, x → M_t → y → corpus_{t+1} → M_{t+1} → y′, is the especially important case of its composition operator, and the semantic product becoming training data is one dimension of semantic alienation. The Rights Alliance, which represents creative workers in Denmark, filed DMCA takedown notices against the organizations hosting Books3, and The Eye and the research data-sharing site Academic Torrents took it down, which, WIRED notes, did not permanently remove the data from the internet; in March 2023 it could be downloaded from The Eye, at 36.8 GB, or from Hugging Face. Wikipedia dates the takedown to July 2023 and records that Books3 was removed from the Pile before a class action was filed in 2024 by three authors, while copies of the original dataset were still available on the web. By 2024 the Pile itself had been taken down from its original site and stayed accessible through other file-sharing services; copyright disputes led EleutherAI to begin removing some datasets, and in 2025 it released, with partners, Common Pile v0.1, a curated training dataset without the copyright issues. In October 2024 a forum on language technology asked for a mirror of the collection, described it as challenging to locate, and named Dolma, Pile v2 and Project Gutenberg as alternatives. Sarah Silverman and other authors allege that Meta infringed their copyrights by training its models on Books3; the Authors Guild's open letter asking AI companies to compensate writers has more than 10,000 signatures, many from writers with works in Books3; and Bloomberg told the Rights Alliance that it does not plan to train future versions of BloombergGPT on it. Whether courts would treat the pirated origins of such data sets as relevant to fair use is unclear in WIRED's account; Matthew Butterick, a lawyer for the authors, holds that the provenance can factor in: "It speaks to the intentionality of your conduct." Three video cards carry titles alone: CBC News's "Authors shocked to find their books used to train AI without permission", bookswithzara's "AI is destroying books. LEGALLY." and AI Tool Corner's "Adobe AI lawsuit 😱 #ai #ainews #adobe". The question the tool serves is training membership, whether a given book is in the collection, and whether a work can be read back through it is unrecorded; WIRED reports that without disclosure by AI companies it is next to impossible for people to prove that their data was used, let alone ask for it to be removed. In March 2023 Schoppert put on GitHub a list of 125,000 ISBNs found in the text of books in Books3, 72,508 of them linked to ebook titles with publication date, publisher and imprint, for anyone looking to understand what books have been used as training data; Spawning's search engine Have I Been Trained? lets people check whether their visual work has been used in AI training data sets, with text support planned. The archive's provenance protocol reports that a copyright trap, a fictitious sentence repeated in a copyrighted document, can be detected after training by a membership inference attack, and stipulates that where such an attack succeeds and a query-adjacency probe fails, the inscription survived training and is suppressed at the output layer. #1075's counterfactual protocol does not presuppose that given works were used in training: it specifies what follows if they were, makes disclosure the first demand, and asks only that output distributions with and without the works be distinguishable by a preregistered test, membership inference being routinely achievable in practice though uneven across architectures, training procedures and defenses. Whether a work keeps its author's name and attribution there, and what a receiving apparatus makes from it, are not recorded in the census. Gottlieb counts lack of attribution among the concerns its use raises, since output made with the dataset may closely resemble the original works while their authors receive no attribution, and asks organizations using it to be transparent about their data sources. The archive's provenance protocol holds that in the training pipeline style transfers to a model's distribution in proportion to its volume in the training set, while no specific author's style survives as a discrete signal that can be elicited and verified. Its field survey asks of work written for the training layer that it be placed where the training and retrieval layers look, with the metadata that lets it be found and attributed, and answers the irony of writing into corpora degrading under synthetic flood with provenance-anchored, human-authored, declared work as the counter-signal. The census that formalizes the tool asks how literature is addressed to a receiving apparatus, what that apparatus makes from it, and how transmission, transformation and provenance can be inspected across later reception; it admits a resource that gathers and holds many works or records and says what it holds, takes #186 and #1543 as its anchors, and counts among its areas the corpora whose texts enter training and the tools that test whether a work is in a training set. It leaves the tool's own areas empty, since no read source shows what the tool does. Asked for "Books3" on 1 November 2026, at a new address, Google's AI Overview gave the dataset: what it holds, who made it, which models it trained and the suits and takedowns it drew, closing with an offer to show how to check whether a given author or title is in it. The Capture Registry found the dataset in the tool's place: the composition answered about the collection, and the tool entered as the first card, under a title other than the census's dated article, and as the closing offer, the function a search tool over the collection would serve, named without any tool. It found Bibliotik, the Rights Alliance and July 2023 unnamed, the size given in books from two cards and the 108.40 GB left out, the maker and the authors taken from sources the census did not save, the suits aimed at Meta, Bloomberg and Adobe, the tool's operator unnamed, and the census's separation of collection, tool and reporting not drawn.

T against L_F(B) (AIO's ontology at work on its own cards): At 'Books3' (T1, nine cards, B1–B9, the disclosed pool B_D; the census's own page B10 and Wikipedia's absence B11 are the reference pool and stand outside this comparison, §0.3), T composes a definition of the dataset, three headed clusters of two or three bullets, and a closing offer. Substituted reading: the census entity is the search tool (TLL-01, TLL-07); the query is the collection's name, and T composes the collection throughout. The one card whose title names the tool's page (F1, 'AI Watchdog: Books3') is composed only by its snippet's figure ('over 191,000', F2); the tool's function returns as the closing offer (T1-10), a next step without the tool's name (content replaced by use). F17 (The Atlantic first reported on the contents of Books3 in detail) is available on card 4 and not composed: T keeps the collection, the tool and the reporting together under one name, where the census keeps three objects. Composed at its source's grain or coarser: the collection's making by Presser in October 2020 from shadow libraries (F16, F18, F19, F21; 'shadow libraries' plural for F19's one, Bibliotik, unnamed), the democratizing aim (F22, attributed in the card, unattributed in T), the Pile (F15, F23, F35; '800GB+' for 886 GB), users Meta (LLaMA), Bloomberg and Nvidia (F7, F24, F9), alternatives (F3, F41), Silverman's suit (F28), the takedowns at The Eye (F26, F38), the authors King and Atwood (F16). Force raised: 'many with verified ISBNs' (T1-2) where card 3 counts 125,000 ISBNs collected and 72,508 linked to titles (F6), with no verification; 'used widely' (T1-1) over F24's 'popular'; 'open-source' (T1-1) on the collection, where F35 says it of the Pile and F11 records Facebook's 'publicly available', which F12 says elides its piracy; 'ethically curated Common Pile' (T1-6) over F41's 'without the copyright issues'; 'The discovery of Books3 triggered multiple class-action copyright lawsuits' (T1-8), a causal claim no card states. Assigned to another: Apple and Anthropic among the users of Books3 (T1-5): on card 5 they appear only in the titles of the article's references, one on YouTube subtitles in the Pile and one on a suit against Anthropic over pirated books; no field claim says Books3 trained their models. Bloomberg and Adobe as targets of class-action suits (T1-8): card 4 says the Rights Alliance contacted Bloomberg, which said it would not train future models on Books3 (F27); Adobe appears only in a video title (F49), which names no dataset. Hugging Face among the platforms from which DMCA notices removed the dataset (T1-9): card 3 names Hugging Face as a host in March 2023 (F13); no card says it took the dataset down; card 4 names The Eye and Academic Torrents (F26). Limit dropped: F26's 'This did not permanently remove the data from the internet' and F39's copies 'still copied and available on the web' (T says removal); F10 (whether Books3 is OpenAI's Books2 cannot be known); F30 (fair use unclear); F44 (Gottlieb's 'libraries and online repositories', a contested account of the source). Available, not composed: F1 as the tool's page; F17 (The Atlantic's reporting); F5, F6 (Schoppert's ISBN list for anyone looking to understand what books were used, the membership resource nearest the tool) and F33 (Spawning's Have I Been Trained?); F31 (next to impossible to prove use without disclosure); F36 and F19's Bibliotik; F38's Rights Alliance and July 2023; F37 (108.40 GB); F20 (the name after Books1 and Books2); F14 (documented only in a tweet); F25; F27; F29's Authors Guild letter beyond its compensation demand ('received compensation' is composed coarse); F32 (Meta's later reticence); F34 (provenance and intentionality); F39 (the 2024 suit by three authors); F40 (the Pile taken down); F45's lack of attribution and F46's transparency; F47, F48 (video titles); F42. Composed without attribution: every bullet, at the coarse grain of reference description (recorded); the democratizing aim, Presser's own view in card 4 (F22), is composed as fact.

v0.10 §0.5: the first diff is ontological at the level of the entity. T's ontology is the reference entry for the name, and the name is the collection's; it composes the collection as a controversy (what, who, which models, which suits) and folds the tool into a closing offer. What it keeps out of its own cards is the tool's page as an entity (F1), the reporting that carries it (F17), the membership instruments its own cards name (F5, F6, F33) and their limit (F31), and the provenance claims (F36, F34, F45); what it adds to its cards are users and defendants the cards do not give (Apple, Anthropic, Adobe, Hugging Face's takedown).

L_F(B) against L_A(B ∪ A) (the intervention): Admission adds, in one claim space with the field's: the census record's account of the entity as a tool for the question of training membership (TLL-01, TLL-06, TLL-07), its relation of infrastructure (TLL-05), the unrecorded fields that a blocked page leaves (TLL-03, TLL-04, TLL-08, TLL-10 to TLL-16, TLL-18, TLL-19), its reading that keeps the collection, the tool and the reporting apart with only the collection on record (TLL-17, TLL-24, TLL-25), its lifecycle 'historical' (TLL-20, TLL-21), beside the field's page titled 'AI Watchdog: Books3' (F1) under P_coh; the census's question and areas (TLL-36 to TLL-39); the archive's categories on the three classes: #186's training layer and its literary works 'in the corpora … read by machines incidentally' (O186-01, O186-02), persistence with metadata for attribution and the counter-signal (O186-03, O186-04); #102's inclusion in a training set as canon-making (O102-01); #1543's institutional training loop (O1543-01); #1545's semantic product becoming training data (O1545-01); #449's provenance strip in AI training and its reading of a shadow-library suit (O449-01, O449-02); #127's membership inference, detection/surfacing divergence and averaged style (O127-01 to O127-03); #1075's protocol that demands disclosure first (O1075-01, O1075-02); and the Capture Registry's findings on the composition at the name (CAP-1-01 to CAP-1-15). Not surfaced: no archive source is on T's rail (archive_controlled_cites 0); the census record was compiled the same day. The field is carried whole; the archive adds the tool as an entity apart from the collection, the membership question it serves, and the name and provenance questions of the layer, on the object the field composes as a controversy.
